we have discovered the first supernova in the act of explosion, marked by a very bright X-ray flash.

the X-ray light curve of the supernova 2011fe shows an extremely luminous (L ~ 10 ^{42} erg/s) outburst that we attribute to the breakout of the supernova blast wave from its progenitor star; the luminosity of this X-ray outburst is comparable to the optical light of the supernova, and the inferred rate of X-ray outbursts is in excellent agreement with the rate of all core-collapse explosions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physics of the most violent events in the universe.
the study of massive stars, and in particular their evolution, and their final fate in supernova explosions.
the study of the physics of supernovae and their progenitors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the progenitors of core-collapse supernovas are massive, hot stars, and that the supernova shock breakout is an X-ray transient.   1
the X-ray outburst is a result of the shock break-out from the surface of a massive star.
the X-ray outburst is the first observation of a supernova in the act of explosion, and the first direct measurement of the rate of such events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the shock breakout is the most luminous X-ray event in the Universe.
we caught a supernova at its birth, in X-rays.
we have found an X-ray outburst that is associated with a supernova, and we can explain this outburst as a result of the shock breakout from the progenitor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
supernovae are not only the brightest explosions in the Universe, but they are also the most luminous X-ray sources.
the progenitors of supernovae are not hidden from view, but are in fact the source of the X-ray emission.
